title: Respiration
subject: Science

opener.question: Think of the last time you ran hard, maybe to catch the school bus or to take a quick single in cricket. Your legs worked very hard for those few seconds. Where do you think that energy came from?
opener.expect: Names food as the source, for example rice, roti or glucose, broken down inside the body. Saying that breathing or oxygen helps is a good partial answer.
opener.answer: It came from the food you ate. Your cells broke it down and set its energy free.
opener.why: Food like rice and roti is broken down into glucose. Your cells break down that glucose, using oxygen, to release the energy stored in it.
opener.hint: Why do you feel weak and tired if you skip lunch and then have to play?

misconceptions.soundsLike: From the air I breathe. The oxygen gives me energy.
misconceptions.why: Oxygen is needed, but on its own it is not the fuel. It helps set free energy that is stored in something else.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you feel that the air itself has the energy in it?

misconceptions.soundsLike: From my heart. It pumps faster and gives my legs energy.
misconceptions.why: The heart is a pump. It moves blood around the body, but it does not make the energy your legs use.
misconceptions.followUp: What do you notice about your heart during a run that makes you think so?

alternates.say: A scooter moves only when there is petrol in its tank. Think about what your body fills its tank with every day.
A chulha gives heat only when wood or gas is burnt in it. Something has to be used up to give energy.

predict.question: Imagine you hold your breath for ten seconds. During those ten seconds, do you think your body stops using energy?
predict.expect: No. The body keeps using energy, because the heart keeps beating and the cells keep working, even though no air moves.
predict.answer: No. Your cells keep releasing and using energy even while you hold your breath.
predict.why: Your heart keeps beating and your cells keep working, so they need energy every second. Holding your breath only stops air moving in and out of your lungs.
predict.hint: While you hold your breath, does your heart stop beating?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Yes. If I am not breathing, no energy is being made.
misconceptions.why: Holding your breath stops air moving, but it does not switch your cells off. There is still oxygen in your lungs and blood for a short while.
misconceptions.followUp: What do you think breathing does for the body that would make the energy stop?

alternates.say: When you sleep, you hardly move at all. Yet your heart beats all night, and you wake up warm.
A van delivers gas cylinders to a house, but the cooking happens on the stove in the kitchen. The van and the stove do different jobs.

points.say: Breathing is only the movement of air. You pull air into your lungs and push it out again, which brings oxygen in and takes carbon dioxide out.

ask.question: So after a hard run, why do you think you breathe faster?
ask.expect: To bring in oxygen faster, and take out carbon dioxide faster, because the working muscles are using more.
ask.answer: Because your working muscles are using oxygen faster, so you breathe faster to bring more in.
ask.why: Hard work needs more energy, and releasing that energy uses more oxygen. Faster breathing brings it in faster and also takes out the extra carbon dioxide.
ask.hint: What does the air you breathe in carry that your hard-working muscles use up?

misconceptions.soundsLike: To take in more carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.why: Carbon dioxide is the gas we breathe out. It is left over after our cells break down food, so the body gets rid of it.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think our body needs to take in carbon dioxide?

alternates.say: Blow gently on a dying coal in an angithi and it glows again. A fire needs a steady supply of air.

points.say: Respiration happens inside every cell of your body. There, food in the form of glucose is broken down, and the energy stored in it is released.

ask.question: So right now, while you sit still and listen, is respiration still going on in your cells?
ask.expect: Yes. Cells respire all the time, even at rest, because the body always needs energy.
ask.answer: Yes. Your cells release energy all the time, even when you sit still.
ask.why: Even at rest your heart beats, your brain works and your body keeps repairing itself. All of that needs energy, every second.
ask.hint: What is your brain doing right now, and does that need energy?

misconceptions.soundsLike: No. Only when I am running or doing some work.
misconceptions.why: Even when you are fast asleep, your heart keeps beating and your body stays warm.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you feel the body needs energy only when it moves?

misconceptions.soundsLike: It is going on only in my lungs, when I breathe.
misconceptions.why: The lungs only take air in and out. The breaking down of food to release energy happens in cells all over the body, even in your toes.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think respiration happens only in the lungs?

alternates.say: A phone lying on the table with its screen off is still using a little battery, just to stay on.

check.question: In your own words, what is the difference between breathing and respiration?
check.expect: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs, taking in oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide. Respiration is the breakdown of food, glucose, inside cells to release energy.
check.answer: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration breaks down food inside every cell to release energy.
check.why: Breathing only brings in oxygen and takes out carbon dioxide. The energy itself is released inside the cells.
check.hint: Which of the two needs your lungs, and which one could go on in a cell of your big toe?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Both are the same thing. Respiration means breathing.
misconceptions.why: In everyday talk people use the words loosely. In science they are two different processes, and they happen in different places.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes them feel like the same thing to you?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Breathing releases energy from glucose, and respiration is taking in oxygen.
misconceptions.why: You have both jobs right, but the two names are swapped round.
misconceptions.followUp: Which one do you think happens in the lungs, and why?

alternates.say: Picture your chest rising and falling. Now picture one tiny cell deep inside your leg muscle. Ask what is happening in each place.

check.question: A fish has no lungs and takes oxygen from water through its gills. Do the cells in a fish's tail still carry out respiration?
check.expect: Yes. Every living cell releases energy from food; gills, like lungs, only take in oxygen.
check.answer: Yes. The gills only take in oxygen, and the tail cells still break down food to release energy.
check.why: Animals get oxygen in different ways, with lungs or with gills, but every living cell has to release energy from food.
check.hint: Does the tail need energy to swish, and where would that energy have to be released?

misconceptions.soundsLike: No. A fish has no lungs, so it cannot respire.
misconceptions.why: Your big toe has no lungs inside it either, yet it is alive and it can move.
misconceptions.followUp: What do you think the lungs have to do with respiration?

alternates.say: First, does the tail move? Next, does moving need energy? Then, where is energy released in any animal?
A tree has no lungs either, yet it stays alive and keeps growing.

teachBack.prompt: Now you be the teacher: explain to your younger cousin why we keep breathing even when we are fast asleep.
teachBack.expect: Cells respire all the time, even in sleep, because the body always needs energy. Respiration in the cells uses oxygen and makes carbon dioxide. Breathing brings the oxygen in and takes the carbon dioxide out.

ideas.title: What goes in and what comes out

predict.question: In photosynthesis, a leaf uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen. When your cells break glucose down again to get its energy, what do you guess comes out at the end?
predict.expect: Carbon dioxide and water, the opposite of photosynthesis, along with energy.
predict.answer: Carbon dioxide and water come out, and energy is released.
predict.why: Breaking glucose down undoes what the leaf built up, so what went into photosynthesis comes back out.
predict.hint: Which gas do you breathe out, and what else does a leaf use up in photosynthesis?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Glucose and oxygen come out, like in photosynthesis.
misconceptions.why: That is what photosynthesis makes. Respiration does the opposite job: it uses glucose up instead of making it.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think the same things would come out of both?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Oxygen comes out.
misconceptions.why: Oxygen is used up in respiration. That is why we have to keep breathing it in.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think oxygen would come out at the end?

alternates.say: Build a small house out of Lego bricks, then pull it apart. Pulling it apart gives you back the bricks you started with.

points.say: Here is the reaction: glucose and oxygen go in, and carbon dioxide, water and energy come out. It runs the opposite way to photosynthesis.

ask.question: So why do you think the air you breathe out has more carbon dioxide than the air around you?
ask.expect: Because cells make carbon dioxide in respiration, as a product, and it is carried to the lungs and breathed out.
ask.answer: Because the extra is made by your cells when they break down glucose with oxygen, and you breathe it out.
ask.why: The blood carries that gas from your cells to your lungs, which is why breathed-out air turns lime water milky faster than room air.
ask.hint: In the equation, is carbon dioxide on the side that goes in, or the side that comes out?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Because we breathe in carbon dioxide and it just comes back out.
misconceptions.why: The air around us has only a little carbon dioxide. The extra must be coming from somewhere inside the body.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think the carbon dioxide just passes through us?

alternates.say: Blow through a straw into lime water and it turns milky quickly. Pump room air through it with a pichkari and it takes much longer.

check.question: At night, with no sunlight for photosynthesis, does a plant still respire, and which gas does it give out then?
check.expect: Yes, plants respire day and night; at night they give out carbon dioxide.
check.answer: Yes. The plant still respires at night, and it gives out carbon dioxide.
check.why: Plant cells need energy all the time, so they respire all the time. At night there is no photosynthesis to use up that carbon dioxide, so it diffuses out of the plant into the air.
check.hint: Does a plant's root cell need energy at night, and what does respiration make besides water and energy?

misconceptions.soundsLike: No. Plants only do photosynthesis, they do not respire.
misconceptions.why: A plant's roots live in the dark soil all the time, yet their cells stay alive and the root keeps growing.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think plants never need to break their food down?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Yes, and it gives out oxygen.
misconceptions.why: A plant gives out oxygen from photosynthesis, and photosynthesis needs light. In the dark, only respiration is going on.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think the plant gives out oxygen even in the dark?

alternates.say: You are asleep at night too, yet you keep breathing out the same gas all night long.

check.question: Tell me the respiration reaction in words: what goes in, and what comes out?
check.expect: Glucose and oxygen go in; carbon dioxide, water and energy come out.
check.answer: Glucose and oxygen go in. Carbon dioxide, water and energy come out.
check.why: The cell breaks down glucose using oxygen. Carbon dioxide and water are what is left, and the energy is released.
check.hint: What is the cell's fuel, which gas does it need to break that fuel down, and what is left over?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Glucose and water go in, and carbon dioxide and oxygen come out.
misconceptions.why: Two of those are on the wrong side. Photosynthesis has them the other way round, which makes them easy to mix up.
misconceptions.followUp: How did you decide which side water goes on?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Carbon dioxide and water go in, and glucose and oxygen come out.
misconceptions.why: That is photosynthesis, where a plant makes glucose. Respiration breaks glucose down, so glucose cannot be what comes out.
misconceptions.followUp: Where have you seen that reaction before?

alternates.say: First name the cell's fuel. Then name the gas it needs to break that fuel down. Then think of what you breathe out, and what photosynthesis starts with.

steps.say: Let us read a similar reaction first, photosynthesis. The plant takes in carbon dioxide from the air through its leaves, and water from the soil through its roots.
Using sunlight and chlorophyll, it makes glucose.
And it gives out oxygen, so in photosynthesis glucose and oxygen are what come out.

teachBack.prompt: Pretend I have never heard of respiration, and tell me how the rice you ate at lunch ends up as the carbon dioxide you breathe out.
teachBack.expect: The rice is digested to glucose. In the cells, glucose combines with oxygen and is broken down into carbon dioxide, water and energy. The blood carries the carbon dioxide to the lungs, and we breathe it out.

predict.question: Glucose can be broken down with oxygen or without it. Which way do you guess gets more energy out of the same amount of glucose?
predict.expect: With oxygen, aerobic, gets more energy, much more.
predict.answer: With oxygen. It gets far more energy out of the same glucose.
predict.why: With oxygen, glucose is broken down completely, all the way to carbon dioxide and water, so much more of its energy is released.
predict.hint: Does a fire in a chulha burn better when you blow air into it, or when you cover it?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Without oxygen, because the cell has to work harder.
misconceptions.why: Working harder is not the same as getting more out. Without oxygen, the glucose is not broken down completely.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think working without oxygen would give more energy?

alternates.say: Squeeze a lemon fully and you get all its juice. Give it one quick squeeze and much of the juice stays inside.
A candle under an upturned glass burns well at first, then grows weak as the air runs out.

points.say: The first step is the same in every kind of respiration. In the cytoplasm, glucose, a six-carbon molecule, is broken into a three-carbon molecule called pyruvate.

ask.question: So if a cell had no oxygen at all, could it still do this first step?
ask.expect: Yes, because the first step happens in every kind of respiration, including the kinds without oxygen.
ask.answer: Yes. Breaking glucose into pyruvate happens in every kind of respiration, even without oxygen.
ask.why: This first step is shared by every pathway, with oxygen or without it.
ask.hint: Did we say anything about oxygen when we talked about this first step?

misconceptions.soundsLike: No. Respiration always needs oxygen.
misconceptions.why: Some living things, like yeast, can respire with no oxygen at all.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think every kind of respiration needs oxygen?

alternates.say: Vegetables are chopped before cooking, whether you cook them on a gas stove or on a chulha. The first step does not depend on how you finish.

points.say: When oxygen is there, pyruvate is broken down in the mitochondria into carbon dioxide and water. This releases a lot of energy, and it is called aerobic respiration.

ask.question: So why do you think the mitochondria are called the powerhouse of the cell?
ask.expect: Because aerobic respiration, the breakdown of pyruvate with oxygen, happens there and releases the most energy.
ask.answer: Because the breakdown of pyruvate with oxygen, which releases the most energy, happens in them.
ask.why: The pathway with oxygen releases far more energy than any pathway without it.
ask.hint: What did we just say happens inside the mitochondria when oxygen is there?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Because they make oxygen for the cell.
misconceptions.why: Mitochondria use oxygen; they do not make it. The oxygen comes in from the air we breathe.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think the mitochondria make oxygen?

alternates.say: A town has many small shops, but one power station supplies most of its electricity.

check.question: Your friend says the energy for running is released in the lungs, because that is where the oxygen comes in: where would you tell your friend it is really released?
check.expect: In the cells of the working leg muscles, mainly in their mitochondria, not in the lungs.
check.answer: In the cells of your leg muscles, mostly in their mitochondria, not in your lungs.
check.why: The lungs only take oxygen into the blood. The blood carries it to your leg muscles, and the mitochondria in the muscle cells use it to release the energy for running.
check.hint: Where does the blood take the oxygen after it leaves the lungs?

misconceptions.soundsLike: My friend is right, it is in the lungs.
misconceptions.why: The lungs are where oxygen enters the blood, but the blood carries it on to every part of the body.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think the energy is released where the oxygen comes in?

alternates.say: Petrol is filled at the petrol pump, but it is burnt in the car's engine.

check.question: Where in the cell is pyruvate broken down using oxygen?
check.why: Glucose is first broken into pyruvate in the cytoplasm. With oxygen, the pyruvate is then broken down into carbon dioxide and water inside the mitochondria.
check.hint: Is it the same place as the first step, or a special part of the cell that releases most of the energy?

misconceptions.soundsLike: In the chloroplast.
misconceptions.why: Chloroplasts are where plants make glucose using sunlight. Animal cells have no chloroplasts, yet they respire too.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think the chloroplast would do this job?

misconceptions.soundsLike: In the nucleus, because it controls the cell.
misconceptions.why: The nucleus controls the cell, but it does not break down food for energy.
misconceptions.followUp: What does the nucleus do that makes you pick it?

misconceptions.soundsLike: In the cytoplasm.
misconceptions.why: The cytoplasm is where the first step happens, glucose to pyruvate. The next step, with oxygen, happens somewhere else.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think it happens in the cytoplasm?

alternates.say: Picture a cell as a room full of jelly. Floating in the jelly are small bean-shaped bodies with folded insides. Which part sounds like a special workshop?

teachBack.prompt: Explain to me, step by step, what happens to glucose in a cell that has plenty of oxygen.
teachBack.expect: In the cytoplasm, glucose, a six-carbon molecule, is broken into pyruvate, a three-carbon molecule. With oxygen, pyruvate is broken down in the mitochondria into carbon dioxide and water, releasing a lot of energy. This is aerobic respiration.

ideas.title: Short of oxygen: lactic acid in muscles

predict.question: In the last over of a match you sprint between the wickets again and again, and your lungs cannot bring in oxygen fast enough. What do you think your leg muscles do then: stop working, or find another way to get energy?
predict.expect: They find another way: they keep going for a while by getting energy without enough oxygen.
predict.answer: They find another way. For a while they get energy without enough oxygen.
predict.why: Muscle cells short of oxygen switch to a pathway that does not need oxygen. They can keep going for a while, but they get much less energy.
predict.hint: At the end of a sprint, when you are out of breath, do your legs stop dead, or can you still push on for a bit?

misconceptions.soundsLike: They stop working. No oxygen means no energy.
misconceptions.why: If that were true, you would collapse the moment you ran out of breath. People can still push on for a while.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think a muscle would stop completely without enough oxygen?

alternates.say: When the electricity goes, many homes switch to an inverter. It gives less power, but the fans keep running for a while.

points.say: When your muscle cells run short of oxygen, pyruvate takes another path. It is changed into lactic acid, which is also a three-carbon molecule, and much less energy is released.

ask.question: Lactic acid still has all three carbons of pyruvate, so how far do you think the glucose was broken down?
ask.expect: Only partly, not completely, not all the way to carbon dioxide and water, which is why less energy is released.
ask.answer: Only partly. It was not broken down all the way to carbon dioxide and water.
ask.why: With oxygen, pyruvate is broken into three separate molecules of carbon dioxide. Lactic acid keeps all three carbons together, so the breakdown stopped early and less energy came out.
ask.hint: With oxygen, pyruvate ends up as carbon dioxide with one carbon each, so is lactic acid broken into pieces that small?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Fully. It was broken down completely.
misconceptions.why: A complete breakdown ends with small molecules like carbon dioxide, each with one carbon. Lactic acid still has as many carbons as pyruvate.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think the glucose was broken down completely?

alternates.say: Picture pyruvate as three beads on one string. With oxygen, the string is cut into three single beads. Now picture lactic acid: how many beads are still on its string?

points.say: During sudden hard activity, lactic acid builds up in the muscles, and this build-up causes cramps. That is why your legs can cramp after a hard sprint.

ask.question: So if you did fast push-ups until you could not do any more, which muscles do you think would build up lactic acid, and why those?
ask.expect: The arm and chest muscles that do the push-ups, because they work hard and suddenly, run short of oxygen and make lactic acid.
ask.answer: Your arm and chest muscles, because they did the hard work, ran short of oxygen and made lactic acid.
ask.why: Lactic acid is made inside the muscle cells that run short of oxygen, and during push-ups those are the arm and chest muscles doing the work.
ask.hint: Which muscles are working hardest while you do push-ups?

misconceptions.soundsLike: My leg muscles, because lactic acid builds up in the legs.
misconceptions.why: During push-ups your legs stay almost still, and lactic acid is made only in muscle cells working hard enough to run short of oxygen.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think lactic acid builds up only in the legs?

misconceptions.soundsLike: In my lungs, because I would be out of breath.
misconceptions.why: Your lungs keep bringing air in the whole time, and lactic acid is made inside the muscle cells that run short of oxygen.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think it would build up where you feel out of breath?

alternates.say: Picture every muscle as its own small kitchen that needs a steady supply of oxygen: the kitchens cooking fastest are the first to run short.

check.question: Two friends cover the same distance, one jogging slowly and one sprinting hard: whose leg muscles are more likely to run short of oxygen and build up lactic acid, and why?
check.expect: The sprinter, because the sprinter's muscles need oxygen faster than breathing and blood can bring it, so they run short and make lactic acid.
check.answer: The sprinter. The sprinter's muscles need oxygen faster than it can reach them, so they run short and make lactic acid.
check.why: The jogger's breathing keeps up with the muscles' need for oxygen. The sprinter's muscles need oxygen faster than it can arrive.
check.hint: Which friend would be panting hard, and what does panting tell you about the oxygen in their legs?

misconceptions.soundsLike: The jogger, because they are running for longer.
misconceptions.why: Both friends' legs keep working the whole way, so what differs is how fast each one's legs use oxygen.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think running for longer would build up more lactic acid?

alternates.say: A tank with a thin inlet pipe keeps up if you open one tap. Open all the taps at once and it runs dry, even though water is still coming in.

check.question: What do your muscle cells make when they run short of oxygen, and what does it cause?
check.expect: Lactic acid, whose build-up causes cramps.
check.answer: Lactic acid. When it builds up in the muscles, it causes cramps.
check.why: Short of oxygen, muscle cells change pyruvate into lactic acid instead of breaking it down fully. Its build-up during sudden activity causes cramps.
check.hint: What three-carbon substance did we say pyruvate turns into in a muscle that is short of oxygen?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Alcohol and carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.why: Alcohol and carbon dioxide are what yeast makes without oxygen. Our muscle cells take a different path.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think our muscles do the same as yeast?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Carbon dioxide builds up and causes cramps.
misconceptions.why: Carbon dioxide is carried away by the blood and breathed out. The cramp comes from something that stays in the muscle.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think the carbon dioxide would stay in the muscle?

alternates.say: Picture pyruvate as three beads on one string: with oxygen the string is cut into single beads, but in a muscle short of oxygen the string stays whole and becomes something new.

teachBack.prompt: Tell me the story of a sprint from your leg muscle's point of view: what happens when the oxygen runs short, and why can it cramp afterwards?
teachBack.expect: Short of oxygen, the muscle cells change pyruvate into lactic acid instead of carbon dioxide and water. Much less energy is released, and lactic acid builds up and causes cramps.

ideas.title: Yeast without oxygen: ethanol and carbon dioxide

predict.question: If you stir yeast into sugar water in a bottle, stretch a balloon over its mouth and leave it somewhere warm, what do you think happens to the balloon, and why?
predict.expect: The balloon swells up, or inflates, because the yeast makes a gas, carbon dioxide.
predict.answer: The balloon slowly swells up, because the yeast gives off carbon dioxide gas.
predict.why: Yeast uses the sugar as food. As it breaks the sugar down, it gives off carbon dioxide gas, which collects in the bottle and fills the balloon.
predict.hint: What would have to be made inside the bottle for a balloon on top of it to change?

misconceptions.soundsLike: It fills with oxygen from the yeast.
misconceptions.why: Oxygen is given out by green plants in sunlight. Yeast is not a plant, and it does not make its own food.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think the yeast would give out oxygen?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Nothing will happen to the balloon.
misconceptions.why: Yeast is alive, and it uses the sugar as food. Living things that break down food give something off.
misconceptions.followUp: What do you think the yeast does with the sugar?

misconceptions.soundsLike: The yeast grows and swells and pushes the balloon up.
misconceptions.why: Yeast cells are far too tiny to fill a balloon by swelling. Only a gas could take up that much space.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think the yeast itself could get big enough to push the balloon?

alternates.say: Bread or pav dough made with yeast, left in a warm place for an hour, becomes bigger and full of tiny holes.

points.say: Without oxygen, yeast changes pyruvate into ethanol, a kind of alcohol, and carbon dioxide, releasing much less energy than with oxygen. This is fermentation, which is anaerobic respiration.

ask.question: So how is what yeast makes different from what your muscles make when they are short of oxygen?
ask.expect: Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide, while muscles make lactic acid.
ask.answer: Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide, while our muscles make lactic acid.
ask.why: Both start from pyruvate without enough oxygen, but they take different paths. Yeast ends with ethanol and carbon dioxide, and our muscle cells end with lactic acid.
ask.hint: What did we say builds up in your legs after a sprint, and is it the same as what yeast makes?

misconceptions.soundsLike: They are the same. Both make lactic acid.
misconceptions.why: Our muscle cells make lactic acid, but yeast takes a different path, and one of its products is a gas.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think yeast and muscle cells would make the same thing?

alternates.say: Picture two roads leaving the same junction, called pyruvate. One road runs through our muscles, the other through yeast, and each ends somewhere different.

points.say: The carbon dioxide from yeast forms bubbles. That is why bread dough made with yeast rises.

ask.question: So why do you think a slice of bread made with yeast has so many small holes in it?
ask.expect: The holes were bubbles of carbon dioxide made by the yeast and trapped in the dough.
ask.answer: The holes were bubbles of carbon dioxide from the yeast, trapped in the dough.
ask.why: The bubbles get trapped in the dough as it rises, and they stay as small holes after baking.
ask.hint: When dough rises, what do you think is taking up the extra space inside it?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Because the alcohol boils and pushes the dough up.
misconceptions.why: The dough rises before it goes into the oven, at room temperature, when nothing is boiling. So something else must be filling it.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think the alcohol boils while the dough is rising?

alternates.say: Look closely at a slice of pav. The holes look like tiny balloons that have been popped.

check.question: If a tube carries the gas from yeast in sugar water into a test tube of lime water, what would you expect to see in the lime water, and why?
check.expect: The lime water turns milky, because the yeast gives off carbon dioxide.
check.answer: The lime water turns milky, because the yeast gives off carbon dioxide.
check.why: Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky. Fermenting yeast gives off carbon dioxide, so the gas bubbling through the tube turns the lime water milky.
check.hint: Which gas did the yeast give off in the balloon bottle, and which test for that gas uses lime water?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Nothing, because yeast only makes alcohol.
misconceptions.why: Yeast does make alcohol, but that is not all it makes. Remember what blew up the balloon.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think the yeast would make no gas?

alternates.say: Think back to the balloon on the yeast bottle. The same gas can be led through a tube instead.

steps.say: Here is a similar test from your chemistry chapter: zinc and dilute sulphuric acid give off a gas.
steps.line: zinc + dilute sulphuric acid → a gas

steps.say: When a burning candle is brought near a soap bubble filled with that gas, the gas burns with a pop.
The pop is what tells us the gas is hydrogen: each gas has a test whose result we can see.

check.question: What does yeast make when it respires without oxygen?
check.expect: Ethanol, or alcohol, and carbon dioxide, with some energy.
check.answer: Ethanol and carbon dioxide, with some energy.
check.why: Without oxygen, yeast changes pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide. This is fermentation, a kind of anaerobic respiration.
check.hint: One product blew up the balloon, so what is the other one that stays behind in the sugar water?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Lactic acid.
misconceptions.why: Lactic acid is what our muscle cells make when they are short of oxygen. Yeast takes a different path.
misconceptions.followUp: Why do you think yeast makes the same thing as a muscle short of oxygen?

misconceptions.soundsLike: Oxygen and water.
misconceptions.why: Yeast uses up food; it does not give out oxygen. Oxygen comes from plants doing photosynthesis.
misconceptions.followUp: What makes you think yeast would give out oxygen?

alternates.say: Our muscles and yeast are two cooks given the same ingredient, pyruvate. The muscle cook makes lactic acid. The yeast cook makes two things, and one of them is a gas.

teachBack.prompt: Imagine your younger cousin asks why bread dough rises: explain it to them using what you now know about yeast.
teachBack.expect: Yeast respires without oxygen, which is fermentation. It makes ethanol and carbon dioxide, and the carbon dioxide bubbles make the dough rise.

prompts: Tell me what goes into respiration and what comes out.
Tell me the three things pyruvate can turn into, and where each one happens.
Tell me, in one line each, how breathing and respiration are different.

facts: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs, while the energy itself is released inside cells when food is broken down in respiration.
Respiration goes on in every living cell all the time, even when we sit still or sleep, because the body always needs energy to keep itself working.
Carbohydrates in rice, potatoes and bread are broken down during digestion to form glucose, the fuel our cells use.
In respiration, glucose combines with oxygen in our cells to give carbon dioxide, water and energy, written as C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy.
Respiration is an exothermic reaction, because energy is given out in it.
In terms of what goes in and what comes out, respiration is the opposite of photosynthesis, which uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen.
The first step in every kind of respiration is the breakdown of glucose, a six-carbon molecule, into a three-carbon molecule called pyruvate, and it happens in the cytoplasm.
With oxygen, pyruvate is broken down in the mitochondria into three molecules of carbon dioxide, and water, and this is aerobic respiration.
Aerobic respiration releases a lot more energy than anaerobic respiration.
In yeast, without oxygen, pyruvate is changed into ethanol and carbon dioxide, and this is fermentation, a kind of anaerobic respiration.
When our muscle cells are short of oxygen, pyruvate is changed into lactic acid, which is also a three-carbon molecule.
A build-up of lactic acid in our muscles during sudden activity causes cramps.
The energy released in respiration is used at once to make ATP, the cell's energy currency, which powers jobs like muscle contraction, making proteins and carrying nerve impulses.
Plants respire too: they exchange gases through the stomata, and the large spaces between their cells keep every cell in contact with air.
At night plants mainly give out carbon dioxide, but in the day the carbon dioxide from their respiration is used up in photosynthesis, so they mainly give out oxygen.
The air we breathe out has more carbon dioxide than the air around us, so it turns lime water milky faster.
